equivalents.note: The Tibetan has 'jigs byed, 'the terrifying one', not a word for the vowel series; paired with dus mtshan ma it matches the usual Tibetan names of Bhairava and Kālarātri, the couple under Cakrasaṃvara's feet, so the translators may have read āli and kāli as that divine pair.
dus mtshan ma, roughly 'night of time' (the usual Tibetan for Kālarātri), reads kāli through kāla, 'time, black', rather than as the consonant series.

The Tibetan seems to split vi-mana, giving mana as sems, 'mind', and vi- as rnam with mi dga', 'not glad' ('Kāṇha's mind is not at all glad'), whereas the Tibetan comment (cp.07.m2) follows Munidatta's 'of distinguished mind' (yid khyad par du 'phags par).
btang snyoms is also the Tibetan for the meditative virtue of equanimity (upekṣā), so the Tibetan line can be read more approvingly than the Bengali 'indifferent, standing apart'.

The Tibetan has 'having come himself' (bdag nyid 'ongs nas) with no word for going, as if it divided abaṇāgabaṇe into āpaṇā, 'oneself', and āgamaṇa, 'coming', rather than reading a pair 'coming and going'.
The same bimana that 1b renders rnam mi dga' is rendered here yid mi bde, 'unhappy in mind', so the Tibetan does not keep the Bengali repetition word for word.
The Tibetan has 'the king's palace', with rgyal po, 'king', where rgyal ba, 'Victor', is the usual word for jina, and pho brang, 'palace', where grong khyer, 'city', would render pura.

Munidatta's Tibetan keeps the song's 'jigs byed both for the lemma ālītyādi ('jigs byed ces bya ba la sogs pa) and in the gloss 'jigs byed ni ye shes kyi snang ba, which equates it with light (āloka).
The gloss dus mtshan ma ni snang ba mched pa equates the song's dus mtshan ma with the spreading of light (ālokābhāsa), matching Munidatta's kālinā lokabhāsena.
The Tibetan reads bde ba chen pos, 'by great bliss', where Munidatta's Sanskrit has sukhena, 'by bliss', so either its manuscript read mahāsukhena or the translators expanded the word.
In the triad body, speech and mind the Tibetan has lus, ngag, yid, using yid (usually manas) for citta rather than sems or thugs.
The comment keeps the song's rgyal po'i pho brang and renders Munidatta's gloss mahāsukhapura separately as bde ba chen po'i grong khyer, so 'city' (grong khyer) appears only in the gloss.
